name: chmod
summary: Change permission bits: who may read, write or execute a file.
compat: Octal digits: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, summed per class (user, group, others): 755 = rwxr-xr-x, 644 = rw-r--r--, 600 = rw-------. Avoid 777: it lets every user modify the file and rarely fixes the real problem.

examples.title: Make a script executable for you
examples.explain: Fixes 'Permission denied' when running ./script.sh. u = owner, + adds, x = execute. Use a+x to allow everyone.
options: Add execute permission for the owner (user)

examples.title: Typical file and directory modes
examples.explain: 644: owner can read and write, everyone else can only read. Directories normally use 755, because x on a directory means 'may enter it'.

examples.title: Protect a private key
examples.explain: ssh refuses keys that other users can read ('UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE'). 600 = only the owner can read and write.

examples.title: Remove group/other write access in a project tree
examples.explain: -R applies the change to every file and directory below <project-dir>. go-w removes write access for group and others, leaving everything else as it was.
examples.warning: Recursive permission changes are hard to undo because the previous modes are lost. Only use it on your own project directory, never on /, /etc, /usr, /home or anything under them as a whole. Check the target with ls -ld first.
options: Remove write permission from group and others

name: chown
summary: Change the owner and group of files (needs root).
compat: Regular users cannot give files away, so chown almost always needs sudo. 'user:' with a trailing colon also sets the group to the user's login group (GNU).

examples.title: See who owns a file first
examples.explain: The third and fourth columns are owner and group. Files created by 'sudo make' or 'sudo cp' end up owned by root, which is a common cause of later 'Permission denied' errors.

examples.title: Give a file back to yourself
examples.explain: $USER expands to your user name; the trailing colon sets the group to your login group.
examples.warning: Runs as root. Make sure <file> is inside your own work directory, not a system file.
options: New owner = you, group = your login group

examples.title: Reclaim a build directory created with sudo
examples.explain: Recursively changes ownership of everything below <build-dir>. Afterwards, build without sudo so it does not happen again.
examples.warning: Recursive ownership changes as root cannot be undone easily. Pointing this at a system directory (/, /usr, /etc, /var) can break the system. Double-check the path with ls -ld first.

name: sudo
summary: Run a single command as root (or another user), if your account is allowed to.

install.note: Embedded images often have no sudo and you log in as root directly. Some distributions use doas instead.

compat: Only prefix sudo when a command really needs it (installing packages, loading modules, editing system files). Building, compiling and running your own programs should not need root.

examples.title: Check what you are allowed to run
examples.explain: Lists the sudo rules for your account. May ask for your password. 'user is not allowed to run sudo' means you need an administrator to add you.
examples.warning: Asks for your password; it only lists rules and changes nothing.

examples.title: Run one command as root
examples.explain: Asks for YOUR password (not root's) and caches it for a few minutes. Only the command after sudo runs as root; redirections like > are still done by your shell (see tee).
examples.warning: The command gets full control of the system. Read it completely before pressing Enter, especially anything copied from the internet.

examples.title: Run a command as another user
examples.explain: Useful for testing what a service account can access.
examples.warning: Acts with that user's permissions; it can still change their files.

name: id
summary: Show your user ID, group ID and the groups you belong to.
compat: Group changes (e.g. after usermod -aG) only show up in new login sessions.

examples.title: Show your identity and groups
examples.explain: uid 0 means root. Group membership decides access to devices such as /dev/ttyUSB0 (group dialout on Debian/Ubuntu, uucp on Arch).

name: umask
summary: Show or set the default permission mask for newly created files.
compat: The mask removes bits: with umask 022, new files get 666 - 022 = 644 and new directories 777 - 022 = 755.

examples.title: Show it symbolically
examples.explain: Prints the permissions new files are allowed to have, e.g. u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx.

name: usermod
summary: Modify a user account; most often used to add yourself to a group such as dialout for serial ports.
compat: Serial devices belong to group dialout on Debian/Ubuntu/Fedora and uucp on Arch. Check with ls -l /dev/ttyUSB0.

examples.title: Check which group owns the serial device
examples.explain: Shows something like crw-rw---- root dialout. Members of that group may read and write the port.

examples.title: Add yourself to a supplementary group
examples.explain: Log out and back in (or reboot) afterwards; existing sessions keep the old group list. Then confirm with id -nG.
examples.warning: Always include -a. usermod -G without -a REPLACES your supplementary groups, which can remove you from the sudo/wheel group and lock you out of administration.
options: Append to the existing groups (only valid with -G)
